questions.q: Per this lesson, what's true of a subgraph that has only been deployed to Subgraph Studio (not published)?
options: It's synced and queryable by its creator, but free, rate-limited, and not visible to anyone else
It's already publicly indexed by The Graph Network's full decentralized indexer set
It cannot be queried at all until it's published
It automatically earns curation signal the moment it finishes syncing
questions.explain: The lesson is explicit: Studio deployment is a staging environment — usable by you, but private and rate-limited until publishing.

questions.q: What does "curation signal" mean in the context of publishing a subgraph, per this lesson?
options: GRT tokens staked on a subgraph to economically incentivize indexers to prioritize indexing it
A rating users leave after querying a subgraph
A required code review step before a subgraph can be published
The number of entities defined in the subgraph's schema
questions.explain: The lesson defines signal as GRT staked to signal to indexers that a subgraph is worth indexing — without it, there's less incentive to prioritize it.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what three concrete things does publishing actually do?
options: Makes the subgraph indexable by the network's decentralized indexers, removes the Studio rate limit, and makes it publicly searchable/queryable in Graph Explorer
Deletes the subgraph from Studio and moves it permanently off-chain
Converts the schema from GraphQL into raw SQL automatically
Changes the subgraph's mapping language from AssemblyScript to JavaScript
questions.explain: The lesson lists these three effects of publishing explicitly, contrasting them with Studio's private, rate-limited, single-indexer state.

questions.q: What three parts make up the production query URL format shown in this lesson?
options: A base gateway URL, an API key, and the subgraph's own ID
A wallet address, a signature, and a nonce
The contract address, the ABI hash, and the start block
A username, a password, and a session token
questions.explain: The lesson shows the exact real pattern: https://gateway.thegraph.com/api/{api-key}/subgraphs/id/{subgraph_id}.

questions.q: In the lesson's example GraphQL query, where do `first`, `orderBy`, `orderDirection`, and `where` come from?
options: They're generated automatically from the schema defined in Lesson 13 — no custom filtering or sorting code was written for them
They must be manually implemented in mapping.ts for every entity
They are special AssemblyScript functions called from within the schema file
They only work if the subgraph was published without curation signal
questions.explain: The lesson states this directly — these query arguments come free from the schema, which is the actual payoff of defining entities well back in Lesson 13.
